newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ostend seeks equal noise rules on Chapter 2 aircraft.
newsitem.headline: Ostend seeks equal noise rules on Chapter 2 aircraft.

text.p: Ostend Airport has called for a level playing field in Europe on the operating rules for old and noisy Chapter 2 aircraft.
Ostend's marketing manager, Paul Walterlot, said that at least ten airlines will be forced to leave under existing regulations on noisier Chapter 2 planes.
A European Union directive, no 9412, stated that all noisier aircraft types, older than 28 years, must leave the airport by January 1, 1998, unless they have a European Union exemption.
The airlines in question have not applied for an exemption at Ostend so will have to leave by January 1, 1998.
Walterlot accuses British and French airports of attempting to lure the traffic away, even though they should be subject to the same rules.
"It seems that the French and British governments are not respecting the European Union regulations as some of their airports are contacting the airlines that are here," he stated.
Walterlot claimed that Stansted, Manston and Vatry,near Reims and Chateroux, south of Paris, were all contacting Ostend's clients in bid to attract them to their airports after the ban takes place.

"How can the airlines go to these airports when they all supposed to be subject to the same regulations? They are not allowed to stay at Ostend. We are supposed to have a unified European ruling on this matter. It is not fair," he stated.
An economical hushkitting system to adapt airlines to Stage 3 standards is not on the market at the moment, he added.
The carriers involved include Middle Eastern, African and U.S. airlines.
Ostend Airport Users Committee will be contacting the Belgian government stating that there is not a level playing field in Europe concerning these rules.
Better news for Ostend is the proposed night ban at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport on some wide-body aircraft.
Some airlines that will have to leave Schiphol will go to Belgium airports such as Ostend, industry sources said.
"The Dutch agents know Ostend well. Around 50 percent of the cargo going through Ostend comes from Dutch forwarders," said Walterlot.
Much of the cargo is vegetables and flowers that pass through the Dutch auctions.

"It will be good if we can replace the carriers we may lose at the end of the year with some of the airlines now using Schiphol." - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
